To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

knickpoints in bedrock catchments are retreating at rates between 0.1 and 2 mm yr-1, and that knickpoint propagation is faster in catchments that are forced by larger tectonic pertubations and that experience more precipitation.
(a) knickpoints retreat faster in areas with high uplift rate and (b) the difference in uplift rate between the two areas is sufficient to explain the difference in knickpoint retreat velocities. [2]

(1) knickpoints retreat faster in areas of higher uplift rate, (2) knickpoint retreat velocities are independent of drainage area for the range of catchments we study and (3) knickpoint propagation rates are higher in Turkey than in Italy due to the higher rainfall to infiltration ratio. [2]
In summary, our research is concerned with
the rate of landscape response to tectonism and climatic change.
the controls on the rate of knickpoint propagation in bedrock landscapes.
how tectonic and climate perturbations are transmitted to the surface through transient knickpoints.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
knickpoints in landscapes with higher rainfall to infiltration ratio have slower knickpoint retreat velocities than those in landscapes with lower rainfall to infiltration ratio.
knickpoint retreat is a function of both tectonic and climate perturbation and that the relative importance of the two is a function of the amplitude of the tectonically induced perturbation.
the response times to perturbation are controlled by a combination of tectonic and lithologic factors, but the relative importance of these factors varies with the type of perturbation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the rate of landscape response to tectonically driven perturbation is controlled by the magnitude of the tectonically induced knickpoint retreat and the magnitude and duration of the perturbation. [2]
catchment response times are controlled by a complex combination of tectonic and hydrological variables.
knickpoint retreat is controlled by both rock mass strength and climate.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the response time of a landscape to a perturbation is a function of the amplitude of the perturbation and the ratio of the perturbation rate to the rate of the natural background process that the perturbation is superimposed on.
tectonic and climate controls on knickpoints are complex and that a simple relationship between the magnitude of tectonic perturbs and knickpoint retreat velocities cannot be assumed.

catchments with high throw rates will have short landscape response times and that these short response times are a function of the magnitude of the tectonically induced change in channel slope and the rate at which sediment is supplied to the channel. [1]
